title: Localized Ukraine Ceasefire Opens Aid Route to Besieged Oleshky
dek: Russia and Ukraine began observing a local truce in the southern city of Oleshky on Tuesday, brokered with U.S. first lady Melania Trump's involvement, as Nordic leaders held their first known call with Putin in years.
author: Meridian Newsroom

image.alt: Flag map of Kherson, the Ukrainian city near the southern front where the localized ceasefire applies

keyPoints: A localized ceasefire began at 3 a.m. Tuesday in and around the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, in Ukraine's Kherson region, to allow an aid and evacuation mission.
The White House said the truce was brokered by first lady Melania Trump, who said it began two days earlier than planned and covers wider areas for humanitarian convoys.
Ukraine's human rights ombudsman said no violations had been recorded by either side as of Tuesday evening, while Moscow kept up missile attacks on other cities.
Finland's president and Norway's prime minister spoke with Vladimir Putin, their first known direct contact since shortly after the 2022 invasion.
body:
Russia and Ukraine began observing a localized ceasefire on Tuesday in and around Oleshky, a devastated city in Ukraine's southern Kherson region that Russian forces occupy. The pause was tied to a humanitarian mission to deliver aid and evacuate residents, and the White House said it was brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump.

## What the truce covers

According to the Associated Press, a local pause in fighting began at 3 a.m. local time to allow the aid mission into Oleshky. Food and medical supplies are running low in the city, where drones and land mines restrict movement for as many as 2,000 people who remain. Russian and Ukrainian negotiators and military officials each confirmed in separate statements that the ceasefire had begun, the AP reported.

Melania Trump said in a post on X that the ceasefire started two days earlier than initially planned "to protect the safety of civilians and to facilitate the delivery of critical humanitarian aid." She said the area covered by the truce extends beyond Oleshky within the Kherson region, to allow safe passage for humanitarian convoys. She did not give further detail on the timing change.

As darkness fell on Tuesday, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, said no violations had been recorded by either side, according to the AP.

## Limits of the pause

The AP also reported that Moscow kept up deadly missile strikes on other cities during the local truce. Earlier attempts at limited ceasefires in the war have unraveled quickly or never took hold, because of deep mistrust between the two sides. The AP noted that both Moscow and Kyiv are keen to win favor with U.S. President Donald Trump after more than four years of war.

Some residents who spoke to volunteers said they feared Russian officials could "filter out" evacuees with pro-Ukrainian views. Russia's occupying forces impose strict limits on who may enter Oleshky, according to the AP.

## Day three: truce holds, aid moves

By Thursday, the truce had entered its third day. Ukraine's ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, and his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova, both said no violations had been recorded. Lantratova said Russian engineers were demining Oleshky's roads to prepare a safe passage for a humanitarian convoy, according to [CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/russia-ukraine-war-drone-dnipro-train-station-oleshky-ceasefire/). The Guardian's live briefing also reported that route demining was under way in the city, where an estimated 2,000 people remain.

Ukraine's Zelenskyy said there had been no massive attacks on the regional capital of Kherson since the truce began, and said a 'huge success' would depend on whether the evacuation of Oleshky went ahead as planned. Officials said local residents could leave for either Russia or Ukraine, but the mechanics remained unclear.

The truce did not stop fighting elsewhere. A Russian drone struck two passenger trains at a station in Dnipro on Thursday, killing at least 14 people and injuring 14 more, officials said. Ukrainian authorities also reported deaths in Chernihiv and Kremenchuk. Russia's Defense Ministry said air defenses downed 1,214 Ukrainian drones overnight, according to [CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/russia-ukraine-war-drone-dnipro-train-station-oleshky-ceasefire/).

A Kremlin foreign policy aide, Yuri Ushakov, said the timing of the next round of three-way talks on a wider settlement was linked to the Middle East conflict and that no date had been proposed, the Guardian reported.

## Nordic outreach to Moscow

In a separate development, Finland's President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre spoke by phone with Russian President Vladimir Putin, officials said. It was their first known direct conversation since shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, according to the AP.

The Nordic leaders described the call as "frank and substantive," Stubb said. Their stated aim was to discuss the war and upcoming trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States, which the AP reported are expected next month in Abu Dhabi. Denmark's prime minister said she was "very skeptical" of reaching out directly to Putin, and said she saw no signs that Russia wanted peace, according to the AP.

Afterward, Støre and Stubb spoke with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, according to his office. The two European leaders said they were speaking for their own countries and not for Europe as a whole.

## What to watch

The key questions are whether the Oleshky mission reaches residents and whether the pause holds through the planned evacuations. Meridian will update this story if the ceasefire is extended, breaks down, or if the trilateral talks are formally scheduled.
